nit: ideally this would be 'psu-sensor:' at the beginning.
Certainly, but may I confirm, should it be prefixed with `psu-sensor` instead of `pwm-sensor`?
Sorry, `pwm-sensor` as you said.  I mis-typed.  My point was to add an identifier as to which piece of code this is touching.
I understand and have corrected it, thank you for the reminder.

I'm a little confused at this.  This is PWM, ie the current output.  waiting for a fan to physically adjust it's speed would be reflected in RPM, the PWM would apply almost immediately.

Can you clarify in your commit message what this means?  Are we waiting for the actual i2c write?  Doesn't that happen in the actual write call?

Some fan control chips have a [programmable] ramp time so that you're not immediately shifting fans from 0 to 100.  This can be important both for acoustic reasons and for current draw reasons.  It might be difficult for your VR to supply the sudden need for additional current necessary for ramping the fans up rapidly.

The MAX31790 datasheet talks about this:

> Because the duty cycle
> ramps to new values at a controlled rate, the values
> in the two registers can be different. See the Register
> Descriptions section for 

This can mean, as Eric wrote, that the "Desired Target PWM" and the "Currently Driven PWM" can be different.

Definitely. This is what I was trying to explain earlier, but rephrased better. It is clear we need to distinguish between the achieved setting (comes from the hardware) versus the desired setting (comes from the user).
This flow is a little bit confusing.  Does the first operation fail?

No, nothing fails from a BMC perspective.  The phosphor-pid-control won't write the PWM (via dbus-sensors) because it sees that the "Currently Driven PWM" matches its desired PWM target, but if the chip is in the middle of a ramp, this "Currently Driven" doesn't match the "Desired Target".  It causes phosphor-pid-control to miss setting the fans.
Yep, you got it. This is another good reason why we need to have visibility into both of them, because they won't always match each other.
Thans for the detailed commit message, Eric!  This is great context.

I am uncertain if this refinement aligns with OpenBMC's definitions and expectations for the `Target` property in the PWM control interface and the `Value` property in the PWM sensor interface.

Additionally, I am unsure if this approach is preferable to implementing driver-specific behaviors within the D-Bus sensor to address the issue.
For instance, handling drivers like [max31790] differently, where the `fan_target` file represents the desired RPM speed instead of PWM.
To calculate the target PWM from the fan_target file, knowledge of the maximum fan tach RPM is required for the conversion.
It's important to consider that the interpretation of sysfs filenames and semantics might differ across drivers, affecting the meanings and relationships of `fan_target` and pwm files.

If there is any guidance or feedback to help determine which method is more appropriate, it would be greatly appreciated.
Thank you very much!

[max31790]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/a33b5a08cbbdd7aadff95f40cbb45ab86841679e/Documentation/hwmon/max31790.rst#L2

Just a friendly reminder to take a look at this commit and provide any feedback if possible.
Your insights would be greatly appreciated.

This is the write function for the Sensor::Value, right?  Why would we not write to the `setValue` property in this case?

It seems like as a result of this code change we don't end up doing anything with the write request, which seems wrong.

Understood. The reason for removing `setValue` was that I believed it necessary to differentiate the nature of the Control::Target and Sensor::Value properties.
However, if it's deemed more appropriate, I can reinstate the call to `setValue`.

The main goal of this commit is to prevent the Control::Target from being directly tied to changes in the driver PWM file, ensuring that it reflects only the value that the user has explicitly written to the D-Bus interface.
May I clarify, does this imply that if we use the Senosr::Value to control the PWM, the Control::Target should also adjust accordingly to reflect the change?

> May I clarify, does this imply that if we use the Senosr::Value to control the PWM, the Control::Target should also adjust accordingly to reflect the change?

If so, could you please let me know if it's possible to directly modify the Control::Target D-Bus property or call the set property for Control::Target here?

I'm happy to make suggestions, but I'm not really sure what you're trying to accomplish.
busctl set-property ... Target 10
busctl set-property ... Target 100
busctl set-property ... Target 10


I would expect to work based on the existing code, does it not?

I have replicated and verified this issue using such consecutive set-property commands.
On a system with the max31790 driver, when executing these commands with the existing code, setting the `Target` to 100 triggers a get `Target` by the PWM sensor.

However, since the max31790 PWM file still reflects 10, the fan sensor updates the `Target` back to 10.
When the `Target` is set to 10 again, it is skipped because it is perceived as unchanged, resulting in the fan PWM actually being set to 100.
Why does the Target 'get' call do anything with the driver?  This is surprising to me.

My initial intent was to centralize all interactions with the driver PWM file under the Control::Target.
As part of that design, I implemented a recovery check on the driver PWM file during the get operation.

However, I now understand that this approach may not be appropriate, so I will remove it.
Done

I don't understand why a property-get turns into driver-write operation.

Please at least add comments as to why this is the case.

Once I have incorporated your suggestions into the current patch and verified that the updated code does not introduce any issues, I will update the patch and revise the comments accordingly.
Thank you very much for your guidance!

+1 to patricks comment.

also, it looks like we've now changed target to be scaled based on min max?

Regarding the scaling of `Target` based on Min and Max, I am unsure if this is the most optimal approach.
I have made adjustments based on the suggestions, and I kindly ask for your guidance.
Thank you very much.

Just a friendly reminder to take a look at this commit and provide any feedback if possible.
I've already made changes based on previous comments.

This is a great idea. I have long been in favor of having more than one readout, one for the user-desired setting, versus another for the hardware-actual setting. The reason is that of fan lag, as you mentioned, and other things such as sensor value quantization. I thought there was an open GitHub issue for this feature request, but there wasn't. It's a good idea. Thanks for adding it.

Thank you very much for your affirmation.
I hope someone can continue to provide feedback or merge this commit.
For systems using the MAX31790, the absence of this commit will prevent the fans from being controlled as expected, which may lead to inaccurate fan-related events or even overheating issues.

> I thought there was an open GitHub issue for this feature request, but there wasn't

There was indeed one issue since 2023 directly related to this issue (https://github.com/openbmc/dbus-sensors/issues/25).

Although we internally chose to modify the max31790 driver to show the user-requested PWM in pwm* file (show MAX31790_REG_PWMOUT register value instead of MAX31790_REG_PWM_DUTY_CYCLE, because pwm* is for setting the desired PWM to the fan, we think it should show back the value we set) as a WA for this issue, I think it can be closed with this patch.
Thank you very much for sharing your experience.
Hi @ed@tanous.net, just a friendly reminder to take a look at this commit and provide any feedback if possible.
Just a friendly reminder to take a look at this commit and provide any feedback if possible.

What's the reason for casting `reqInt` back to a double (after losing information through rounding) over using `req` directly?

It seems noisy and odd.

Hi @andrew@codeconstruct.com.au,

You’re absolutely right that `reqInt` is only used to avoid floating-point equality comparisons, and that `targetValue` should be calculated directly from `req`.
I’ve updated the patch accordingly.

Please let me know if there’s anything else in this commit that needs to be addressed to make it merge-ready.

Thank you very much for your feedback!
